blocks.title: Vernalisation
blocks.text: Biennial and perennial plants are stimulated to flower by exposure to low temperature; this is vernalisation. The low-temperature stimulus is received by the shoot apex of a mature stem or by the embryo of the seed, not by the leaves as in photoperiodism.

For some plants vernalisation is an absolute requirement; in others it simply assists in inducing flowering. The duration of the low-temperature (chilling) treatment varies from four days to three months, and a temperature of about 4 degrees Celsius is very effective. It stimulates the production of a hormone, vernalin, which induces vernalisation.

Photoperiodism and vernalisation synchronise the reproductive behaviour of plants with their environment, ensuring reproduction at favourable times of year. They also ensure that the members of a species flower at the same time, encouraging cross-pollination and so genetic variability.
